    {
     "subtitle": "History leaves the academic halls: why Krešimir Rotim stepped in front of the cameras",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim in the TV Jadran studio explains how he moved history from academic circles into the media",
     "content": "The host opens the show „Pogled s Markovog trga“ from the Zagreb studio of TV Jadran by introducing the guest, **Krešimir Rotim**, whom he calls a young historian. The host says that he gladly listens to him because he speaks „briefly, but concisely“. He himself admits that he is inclined to long and broad presentations, so he invites the guest to speak somewhat longer this time. He adds that he usually imagines historical guests as older gentlemen, and that people recognize Rotim immediately, as soon as his name is mentioned.\n\nIn the host's opinion, the reason is that Rotim moved history from „university chairs, salons and closed spaces“ into the *mainstream* and under the spotlights. He asks him whether this was the intention or whether it happened spontaneously.\n\nRotim answers that he himself is part of the academic community: he studied history, wrote quite a few scientific articles and books and took part in academic debates, although, as he says, he is still young and has time to leave his mark on the scientific community. However, he saw that certain arguments do not get through and that certain narratives do not pass. He invoked the legal principle that the other side must also be heard, which has not been heard until now.\n\nRotim points out that technologies have changed the way of fighting: once it was the pen, and today it is video and longer-format shows. These, he says, give the opportunity to present in an argued and much deeper way what arises from „in-depth analysis“ and, as he stresses, **archival material**. He believes that the first duty of a historian is to exhaust the archival material. He reproaches „mainstream“ historians for trying to keep Croats in a „tense atmosphere of guilt“ without doing such work. As an example he mentions the Vukić–Goldstein debate, in which, he claims, a serious geopolitical and historiographical question was trivialized. He concludes that the new media are an opportunity for people to hear that history is not the way they were taught for decades and that there is also a „Croatian side of history“.",

     "subtitle": "Thirty-six years of independence, and history still in the Yugoslav mold",
     "screenshot_description": "The host speaks about the coincidence of the Croatian mainstream with the Serbian narrative",
     "content": "The host assesses that it is „fascinating“ that Croatia, after **36 years of independence**, still remains within the framework of the Yugoslav historical paradigm, which he describes as „reinforced“. This framework, according to his words, also carries the infamous „guilt of Croats“ and the related wars.\n\nThe host stresses that these narratives are almost identical to the Serbian mainstream and to what is said daily in Serbia. He speaks about „auto-chauvinism“, which he calls an almost sick condition and a psychological war. He announces that examples will show how far this can go, all the way to „the recent Zafranović“, and how dangerous it can be.\n\nHe also recalls the generational experience: his generation, he says, saw how Television Belgrade and the Belgrade media contributed to the war starting in 1990/1991. In doing so he announces that this will be discussed later in the show.",

    {
     "subtitle": "Revisionism is not a curse word: „It is the foundation of every science“",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim explains why revisionism is the foundation of historical science and how it has been stigmatized",
     "content": "The host asks a question which, he says, is present in the public: all scientists are allowed to do revision, except when it comes to Croatian history. As soon as someone says that something should be studied further, he is immediately declared a revisionist, as if he were „the worst enemy of the state and the party“. He asks the guest to remove the negative prefix from the term and to explain how important revisionism is.\n\nRotim answers that revisionism is the **foundation of every science**, and especially of historical science, which is burdened by politicization, particularly when it comes to the Second World War, the postwar period and the communist period. According to his interpretation, Stalin „consciously and for the defense of the Soviet regime“ introduced the concept of anti-fascism and thereby contaminated the debate, which continues to this day. Rotim claims that for this reason it is not even possible to make a historical overview of how Bolshevism, that is, communism, earlier viewed fascism. According to him, Stalin „cunningly crossed over to the side of the Western allies“ and thus morally legitimized himself in victory.\n\nRotim recalls that without revision there would be no numerous scientific discoveries or general historical overview. He describes the stigmatization of revisionism as „a method of disqualification and nothing else“, and he includes in its spread the media, which have a „soft power of persuasion“. He believes that the stigma should be removed with new, creative approaches: to go out in front of people and concisely present arguments to them, so as not to remain in the „infamous Croatian silence“.",

     "subtitle": "Croatian silence and the refusal of a showdown: why the other side does not dare to debate",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim speaks about the refusal of public debate and unpleasant reactions to his work",
     "content": "The host connects „Croatian silence“ with the notion of „geese in the fog“, which he calls awkward notions that Croats still cultivate. He describes Rotim as a person who openly expresses his views, which provokes strong reactions from the other political pole. He asks him whether it is hard to deal with ugly comments on a personal level, although, according to the host, they only show how the other side functions.\n\nRotim says that comments, especially those coming from „eastern neighbors“, mostly make him laugh, but that it can be unpleasant when someone tries to discredit him professionally and has not come out to a showdown with him. As an example he states that **Hrvoje Klasić** refused a debate, and he believes that others will not dare to come either after Goldstein's experience. He assesses this as „very bad“, because, he says, the foundation of democratic life is sitting at the same table. He describes himself and his colleagues as „very decent“ people who do not come to cause scandal, but to revive historical moments from Croatian past, study them and draw conclusions for the present.\n\nIn Rotim's words, the task of historians is to remove the „propaganda of horror“ that exists around certain areas of Croatian history. He regrets that the left, which was once inclined to debates and had a notion of progress, is today „blackmailed“ and without the will for the mental effort needed to prepare a public debate. He says that he does not see more serious historians who have diligently prepared and are ready to come out to a public debate and, in the „manner of the best democracy and good human will“, gather around the interest of the Croatian people.",

     "subtitle": "The continuity of Greater Serbian policy and the dismemberment of the Banovina Hrvatska",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim explains plans for the division of Croatia after the Cvetković–Maček agreement",
     "content": "The host claims that the 20th century was key in Croatian history, a kind of „resolution of all struggles, desires and failures“, among them the failed Croatian policies. The period between the two wars, of the Kingdom of SHS and then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, according to him clearly shows everything that would later happen, but also the **continuity of a certain policy**. He refers to conversations with the historian **Tihomir Rajčić**, an expert on Serbian policy up to the First World War. According to the host, Rajčić often repeats that the ideas from the nineties were established in the Serbian political top even before the First World War. Therefore, he concludes, history should be learned with understanding, not by heart. He also warns that the NDH is often discussed fragmentarily, so a wrong story is created from fragments.\n\nThe host states as a starting point the year 1939 and the **Cvetković–Maček** agreement, by which the **Banovina Hrvatska** was created on 26 August 1939. According to him, a special atmosphere then arises in Croatia, but at the same time the „log revolution“ also begins.\n\nRotim continues that after the agreement and the creation of the Banovina the process went in the direction of the **dismemberment of Croatia**. The role intended for Croats, he says, is clearly described by the documents of the Chetnik movement of Draža Mihailović. He admits that this is another matter and that this movement later split and did not have great strength. Still, he considers it unfair to enter the context of the Second World War only with 10 April and the arrival of National Socialist Germany and Fascist Italy. He adds that nobody today disputes the right to a state despite National Socialist evil, and that Stalin's order until 22 June 1941 is responsible for the death of millions of people. In doing so he stresses that every death of innocent people is too much and that the two totalitarian orders are incomparable.\n\nRotim speaks about „Serbian conspiratorialness“, which he connects with a different historical experience under Ottoman rule, from which, he says, political and cultural elites arose. According to his interpretation, even when it was written in the agreement that districts with a Serbian majority would go to the Serbian side, this was not enough: Croats should remain in their enclave, and „then we will see“ what to do with them. For Muslims, he claims, the solution was even worse because they are politically and numerically weaker and militarily unorganized. Vlatko Maček's policy, he notes, was not sufficient even when Croatian deputies were shot at in the Belgrade parliament. He concludes that after everything nobody reasonable would say that anything should be inherited from the common coexistence with Serbs.",

     "subtitle": "The crooked start of the common state: from the December victims to the assassination in the assembly",
     "screenshot_description": "The host speaks about researching the assassination in the Belgrade assembly and the 6 January dictatorship",
     "content": "The host describes that the common state began „crookedly“, although, as he adds, not equally for everyone. He recalls **5 December 1918** and the December victims, when, he says, ordinary people in Zagreb rose up against what they felt was coming. He also mentions Ante Trumbić, who in 1920, when he realized that Pašić and Karađorđević were handing serious Croatian territories to Italy, „hits his head against the wall“ and becomes aware.\n\nThe next impulse of this awareness, according to the host, was the **assassination in the Yugoslav Assembly**. He recounts that in 2018, on the occasion of the ninetieth anniversary, he tried to research this topic in Belgrade. He went through the Old and the New Assembly, asked and begged, but found no trace anywhere. He concludes that for Serbian, that is, Belgrade historiography it simply did not happen.\n\nHe then mentions the assassination of King Alexander I and the **6 January dictatorship**. According to his words, during the Yugoslav dictatorship Serbian gendarmes killed about three thousand Croats, from Lika to Hercegovina. It is precisely in such circumstances, he says, that the NDH appears, which, like Tuđman, he describes as an expression of the Croatian aspiration for its own statehood.",

     "subtitle": "April 1941: taking over power without revenge and a „spiritual awakening“",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim lists examples of taking over power and the disarming of the Yugoslav army in the NDH",
     "content": "The host asks about the advantages and shortcomings of the NDH: Croats, after centuries of bleeding through wars, in a combination of circumstances received a state. In what was that state good, and in what did it err?\n\nRotim admits that the question is very complex and that it should be broken down „layer by layer“. He starts from Tuđman's definition of the NDH as an expression of the aspiration of the Croatian people for a state. He lists a series of examples of taking over power: the Bjelovar uprising, Zagreb, places in the Drava region, Hercegovina, Dalmatia, Slunj. According to him, everywhere the Yugoslav army was disarmed, **there were no civilian casualties**, there was no revenge, and power was taken over before the arrival of the Germans.\n\nAs a positive side he states the **spiritual and cultural awakening** of those years. Although it was a wartime state and the Ustaše tried to ideologically take over almost all the threads of power, cultural life nevertheless came alive, books were printed, people wrote about Croatian history, and Croatianness was lived in everyday life. The Catholic faith was professed, and Orthodoxy, as he says, as a project of the Karađorđevićs and Serbian royal power, lost power in the political sense.\n\nAt the same time he immediately goes to the negatives: the Orthodox were at one point outside the law, until the official authorities called them „Greek-Easterners“ (in the transcript: „Greek and Easterners“).",

     "subtitle": "The Jewish question and racial legislation: „It remains on our collective conscience“",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim speaks about racial legislation, the deportations of Jews and the motives for passing the laws",
     "content": "Rotim asks right at the beginning that two questions be separated: the **suffering of Jews** and the **Serb question** in the NDH. He claims that Serbs „cunningly mix“ these two questions and enter the topic of the Holocaust in order to accuse Croats. He notes that an anti-Jewish spirit existed throughout Europe, but that it should not be confused with the racial-biological, racist teaching about a lower race. As for the suffering of Jews itself, he says the matter is indisputable. The host adds that there were also Jews in the Ustaša movement, from Frank onward. Rotim adds, for the sake of historical truth, that the main periodical of the Jewish community in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia did not support King Alexander, that is, that the relationship was twofold.\n\nThe host explicitly says that the Holocaust „cannot be justified in any way“ and asks whether the adoption of racial laws was a mistake. Rotim answers that, as an explanation, from statements and testimonies from April and May up to the passing of the laws, it is offered that the laws were passed primarily as a replica of the Viennese laws, in order to come closer to the Germans. Croats, he stresses, were then fighting for their living space, that is, Dalmatia. Mussolini recognized the NDH, but on the condition of negotiations on future borders. Rotim concludes from this that Pavelić promised him nothing, so he assesses the claim from Yugoslav historiography that Dalmatia was sold in advance as incorrect.\n\nAccording to Rotim, wartime legislation was also motivated by the wish for a more favorable position in future negotiations with the Italians over Dalmatia and Istria. At the same time he admits that a strong anti-Jewish climate existed, which was fertile ground for the passing and implementation of the laws, and that this is something that the national conscience must overcome. The implementation was not complete, but a large part of the Jewish community was deported to Auschwitz. Rotim calls this a matter that remains on „our collective conscience“, despite the presence of National Socialist Germany as the then official ally.",

     "subtitle": "27 March 1941: Belgrade protests and the attitude toward the Banovina Hrvatska",
     "screenshot_description": "The host speaks about the protests of 27 March 1941 in Belgrade and about the photograph of Chetniks with banners",
     "content": "Rotim moves on to the Serb question and claims that the **propaganda war** on the part of Serbia and the SPC began very early, in the first months of the NDH, when there were still no civilian casualties. The host interrupts him at this point and asks to go back several months, because, as he says, history does not begin on 10 April.\n\nThe host recalls **27 March 1941** in Belgrade and General Simović. He states that Ivo Andrić, as ambassador of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia in Berlin, conveyed to Hitler the decision that Yugoslavia is joining the Tripartite Pact, which according to the host shows that Belgrade had decided to stand with Germany even before 10 April. He also mentions the official thesis that the demonstrations of 27 March were started by British agents.\n\nThe host says that Yugoslav historiography always showed the photograph with the banner „Better war than pact“. While studying in America he saw, he says, the whole picture, in which Chetniks can be seen going with banners into Croatia, that is, toward the destruction and burning of the Banovina Hrvatska. He concludes that the official Belgrade attitude toward Croatia did not begin on 10 April, but lasts much earlier and culminated on 27 March. Had Belgrade not been bombed and Yugoslavia not collapsed, they were, he claims, ready to set out to destroy the Banovina Hrvatska.",

     "subtitle": "Closed Belgrade archives, open NDH boxes and the role of the SPC",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim calls on critics to open the NDH archive boxes and find incriminating documents against Stepinac",
     "content": "The host and Rotim agree that the truth about this should be sought in the West, in the archives in England and Washington. Rotim notes that the Belgrade archives are **still not accessible**, and the host wonders why.\n\nRotim addresses the critics who in the days before the show, primarily on the social network X, directed insults at him: some, he says, are only a few hundred meters from the archive, where „over 500 boxes of the NDH“ are located. He calls on them to pull out the documents that incriminate Stepinac, points out that there are minutes of the sessions of the Doglavnik Council and the Ustaša Main Headquarters, and asks that they show him „all the incriminating data“. The host adds that the other side is allowed to base the building of the myth on Ustaša historiography, while Croats are denied the right to the documents.\n\nRotim states that the Slovak ambassador in Belgrade after 27 March assessed that the events look like a renewal of Greater Serbia, and not like Yugoslav resistance. He also mentions that the Croatian Club of Deputies, after the killings in the Belgrade assembly, warned of the radicalization of the political scene, while nobody answered for the arrival of the gendarmes and the killing of people, and Croats, as he says, „paid for their own bullets“.\n\nRotim describes Greater Serbian policy as long-lasting: from the 19th century, after Serbs were driven out under Ottoman rule, work was done on the unification of all Serbs in one country, and in this the **Serbian Orthodox Church** „wholeheartedly helped“ them. Therefore, according to him, it is not about „decent people“ with whom things are settled at the table, but about hidden motives. According to Rotim, from 10 April this activity also starts in Dalmatia: Niko Novaković Longo sends the Italians a petition with the wish to separate Dalmatia, and in Belgrade the Germans are asked to introduce military administration. Rotim announces a serious research question about the role of the German intelligence community and SS men in creating the atmosphere of „propaganda of horror“ in the first months of the NDH. He also says that if Croatian institutions truly worked in the Croatian spirit, the story could be rationally unified, but for now it remains on the enthusiasm of historians.",

     "subtitle": "Uprisings of 1941 and Srb: ethnic cleansing of the Croatian population",
     "screenshot_description": "The host describes the events in Srb on 27 July 1941 and the destruction of Catholic parishes",
     "content": "The host describes a „succession of moments“ in the area of the then NDH, which covers part of today's Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were a number of enclaves in which uprisings, non-recognition of Ustaša rule and violence against the civilian Croatian population occurred, which was later used as justification for Ustaša terror against the Orthodox and Serbian population in the first months.\n\nAs a key event he states **27 July 1941 in Srb** and what followed until October 1941. According to him, a whole series of Catholic parishes was eradicated in that area, for example in Grahovo and further north, toward the northwest, and this is, he says, „classic ethnic cleansing“. The host claims that the background is clear: Belgrade, manipulating Serbs in Croatia, under no circumstances wants to recognize a Croatian state, however democratic it might be, not even as the SR Croatia. According to him it is not about partisan advances, but about a pure rebellion against the Croatian state, in which the Partisans sign agreements with the Chetniks and Italians, with a „mish-mash of influences“.\n\nRotim adds that it is a total war that begins after the first months of consolidation of power, when the disarming of the Yugoslav army was not yet finished. He also states that the communist authorities committed mass shootings in Tezno, comparing this, with a reservation about the „Kutina Forest“, with Katyn. The rebellion, according to him, is confirmed by books, diaries, proceedings and memoirs of communists, and Drvar was „carefully and in a planned way“ prepared.",

     "subtitle": "Refused surrender of weapons and the children's flight: „The first humanitarian catastrophe“",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim speaks about the first flight of children toward Bihać and their care",
     "content": "Rotim claims that the preparation of the armed rebellion can be seen in the fact that former Yugoslav soldiers, sent back to their homes after the collapse of the army, for months did not want to hand over their weapons, which he interprets as planning „something of this type“. This, according to him, corresponds to the „Serbian mentality of solving problems by armed means“. With this he introduces the topic of Jadovno and the Kozara children.\n\n**The first humanitarian catastrophe**, especially the one that struck children, Rotim regards as a product of the rebellion in Srb. Children from Croatian regions and from Boričevac went toward Bihać, and then further. A column of civilians, mostly women and children, was exposed to Chetnik gunfire, and a large number of people were killed. Many children were left without parents. Rotim says that this example shows how the authorities of the NDH treated children without parents. Living conditions were much worse than before, especially because of food and transport, since the railway, the main route for transporting food, was often under the control of rebels or exposed to sabotage.\n\nIn that flight, according to Rotim, an attempt was made to help the children: a series of state institutions placed them in homes and among families, **without distinction between Croatian and Muslim children**. As one of the worst consequences of the rebellion he states the massacre in the Ivezić family, in which children of several years of age were thrown into a pit. He regrets that today's Croatian authorities allow this to be celebrated as an uprising.\n\nThe host assesses that it is ethnic cleansing with all the elements of genocide. Rotim states that some parishes, among them Vrtoče and Krnjeuša, disappeared completely, and the host adds that people were killed, slaughtered and thrown alive into pits. According to Rotim, the Ustaša garrison in Gospić was not attacked, and the rebels, as can be seen from the diaries of prominent communists, waited until they felt ready. The host concludes that the general goal was the destruction of the Croatian people by cleansing the area of the tri-border region, and Rotim that from that moment that area became „SAO Krajina before SAO Krajina“, without access for Croatian authorities.",

     "subtitle": "Italian rule in Split and Dalmatia: how fascism gave birth to resistance",
     "screenshot_description": "The host and Rotim talk about the Italian occupation of Split and unfulfilled agreements",
     "content": "Before continuing, the host wants to touch on the „truly negative effects of the NDH“, especially for Dalmatia and Split, where people, according to his words, „fared very badly, like Istria“. He believes that Dalmatia and Istria were thrown into the hands of the Italians, so it is no wonder that the resistance movement, later called Partisan, including the Split detachment, gained such numbers: under the Italians, he says, one could not live, and in Split „gigantic fascism“ was felt. The host asks why the dual rule, Italian and Croatian, which was talked about in the negotiations, was not realized, and why Split did not receive a Croatian part of the rule.\n\nRotim answers that **Mussolini did not keep to the agreements**. The Fascist „predators“, he claims, after the defeat in the African colonies wanted to prove themselves and achieve the expansion of the planned Roman Empire. Totalitarian regimes, he says, think that they are „undoubted historical progress“; fascism tried to use its chance and, although militarily it was not particularly successful, it caused enough confusion.\n\nRotim says of the NDH that on the one hand he sees **unnecessary reprisals and crimes**, because of which part of the people identifies Ustaša rule with the Croatian state. The host agrees that this should be separated: Croats, he says, are a peaceful people, and the creation of camps or the killing of people is not an expression of the Croatian spirit. Rotim adds that in the apparatus and the army there were many Croats of various political convictions and that the state had to be preserved, because without a state and protection the catastrophe of Bleiburg happened, about which the story is still being told even 80 years later.",

    {
     "subtitle": "The Rome Treaties and 200 thousand Italian soldiers: „As much was achieved as could be“",
     "screenshot_description": "Rotim explains the influence of Italian military pressure on the Rome Treaties",
     "content": "Rotim calls the Italian presence the second „millstone“: in those areas, according to him, there were about **200 thousand Italian soldiers**, and this military pressure and strength caused the Rome Treaties, on which the then authorities could not influence much.
